name: Vaser liposuction

lead: VASER is a brand of ultrasound-assisted liposuction. It uses ultrasonic energy to loosen fat before it is suctioned out and is widely associated with high-definition liposculpture, which aims to show muscle outlines such as the abdominals.
Published work is largely surgeon-reported case series, with a few small comparative trials against conventional suction liposuction.

paras: A probe delivers ultrasonic energy into the fat layer, and the fat is then aspirated. Surgeons describe work on superficial fat as the basis of definition procedures.

Liposuction in general carries reported risks including infection, bleeding, blood clots, organ perforation and fat embolism, with risk rising with volume removed. A dedicated review covers complications of high-definition liposculpture.

lead: VASER (vibration amplification of sound energy at resonance) liposuction is a form of ultrasound-assisted liposuction in which a probe delivers ultrasonic energy to fat before it is suctioned out. It is described in the surgical literature as a third-generation ultrasound technique, introduced after earlier ultrasound devices that surgeons reported as bulky and associated with a higher potential for complications.[1][2]

In appearance culture it is best known as the tool behind high-definition liposculpture, sometimes called abdominal etching, in which fat is removed or shaped to emphasise the outline of muscle groups such as the abdominals. Surgeons who developed the approach reported using VASER to treat superficial fat layers and to define musculature as well as to reduce volume.[3][4]

Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon-reported case series and a small number of comparative trials against conventional suction-assisted liposuction. Liposuction in general is described as removing fat locally without producing lasting weight loss.[5]
infobox: Vibration amplification of sound energy at resonance

paras: VASER is a brand of ultrasound-assisted lipoplasty. Ultrasonic energy applied through a probe in the fat layer is intended to loosen fat so it can be aspirated, and authors of early reports compared it with earlier ultrasound-assisted devices as well as with conventional suction.[2] A general overview of liposuction notes that 1980s and 1990s ultrasound devices sometimes injured tissue through excess ultrasound exposure, while third-generation devices use pulsed energy and specialised probes.[5]
Surgeons describing the technique say it allows work on the superficial fat layer, which is the basis of high-definition approaches that aim to show muscle detail instead of only reducing bulk.[3]

A 2007 report described VASER-assisted high-definition liposculpture as a way to improve contour and highlight underlying musculature, extending earlier differential lipoplasty techniques that had been limited to small areas in lean male patients.[3] Abdominal etching more broadly was first described in 1993.[5]
A 2018 report described 736 high-definition lipoabdominoplasties performed with circumferential VASER liposuction between 2005 and 2017, combining abdominal definition with abdominoplasty.[4]

A 2002 pilot clinical study reported on VASER-assisted lipoplasty and compared its outcomes with those of other ultrasound-assisted devices.[2] A multicentre, prospective, randomised, single-blind trial published in 2012 used a contralateral design in 20 female patients to compare VASER-assisted and suction-assisted lipoplasty, and its authors noted that no earlier comparative study had shown a statistically significant benefit of a new technology over suction-assisted lipoplasty.[6] A registered trial of 21 participants compared the two approaches.[7]

Other published work includes a comparison of blood loss between suction-assisted and third-generation ultrasound-assisted lipoplasty,[8] a study of acute fat-cell viability after third-generation ultrasound liposuction,[9] and a review of complications of high-definition liposculpture and how they are managed.[10] A trial comparing adipose viability after liposuction is registered as recruiting,[11] and a registered study is evaluating rib osteotomy for waist narrowing as a separate body-contouring approach.[12]

Liposuction in general is described as considered safe but with risk that rises with the volume removed. Reported serious complications include deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding, infection and fat embolism, and deaths have been estimated at about one per 10,000 cases as of 2011.[5] Early ultrasound devices were reported to carry additional potential for tissue injury and complications.[2] A dedicated review addresses complications specific to high-definition liposculpture.[10]
